729.title: Sri Chand the ascetic
729.hook: Nanak's elder son chose a celibate life; the Udasi order traces itself to him
729.howItsDone: Sikhs follow the householder path the Gurus taught, and they remember Baba Sri Chand with respect as Guru Nanak's elder son and the figure the Udasi order traces itself to.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mata Sulakhni, and your line, the one who stayed. Did your thanks reach the person who kept home going? Day seven hundred twenty-nine.

A family business, three generations in. The father built it. Everyone assumes the eldest will take the keys. But the eldest's heart is somewhere else, and in the end the keys go to someone outside the family. Nobody is disowned. Families know this scene. Guru Nanak's family knew it too. Yesterday we met Mata Sulakhni and her two sons. Today we follow the elder one, Sri Chand, who chose a life his father didn't choose. Today's word: Udasi.
screen: `THE ELDEST SAYS NO.` → `A ROAD OF HIS OWN.` → `TODAY: SRI CHAND.`

segments.voice: Sri Chand grew up while his father was out on the long road. And he grew into a man drawn to stillness and renunciation. Tradition remembers him as an ascetic: celibate, living apart from the household, devoted to meditation. He never married. And the Udasis, an order of renunciants, trace themselves to him. Udasi is a word Sikhs already know from Nanak's own life, because the Guru's great journeys are called his udasis. So the son's order carries a name that echoes the father's travels. Here's the tension, and the tellings don't hide it. Guru Nanak's own way, as his hymns describe it, was the householder's way: earn honestly, share, remember God in the middle of family and work. He came home to Kartarpur, to the fields and the family. And when it came time to choose who would carry the light after him, he didn't choose either son. He chose Lehna, and named him Angad. Sri Chand went another way. So what do the stories know? They hold two things at once. Sikh teaching follows the householder path the Gurus walked. And tradition still remembers Sri Chand with honor, as Baba Sri Chand, the Guru's son, a man of deep devotion who took a different road. Tradition remembers later Gurus and Sri Chand meeting with respect. Udasi teachers, tradition says, went on honoring Guru Nanak and singing his word. That is how respect for a different choice looks in a family of faith: you don't pretend the roads are the same, and you don't stop calling each other family.
screen: `A SON DRAWN TO STILLNESS.` · `UDASI, AN ECHO OF THE JOURNEYS.` · `THE HOUSEHOLDER'S PATH, AND ANOTHER.` · `REMEMBERED WITH HONOR.` · then, large: `A DIFFERENT PATH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: respect a different choice. Settle and breathe. Bring to mind someone close who chose a road you didn't. A sibling who left the faith, or entered it more deeply. A child who took a different job, a different city, a different kind of life. A friend who stayed single, or married young. Notice the old argument that rises. Don't try to settle it. Just look at them, choosing, and find one thing in their choice you can honestly honor. If you pray, you can say Waheguru with them in mind. The bell holds the time.
Udasi. The order of renunciants that traces itself to Baba Sri Chand, Guru Nanak's elder son, and a name that echoes the Guru's own journeys.
Your line: a different path. Today, tell that person one thing you respect about the road they chose, without adding a but. Day seven hundred twenty-nine.

730.title: Home to Talwandi
730.hook: tradition says his parents begged Nanak to stay; he told them his work was on the road
730.howItsDone: Sikhs tell the sakhi of Guru Nanak's return to Talwandi, his birthplace, now Nankana Sahib, as a story of love for family held together with the call to travel and teach.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Udasi, and Sri Chand's road, and your line, a different path. Did you tell someone what you respect about the way they chose? Day seven hundred thirty.

The airport arrivals hall. A mother on her toes behind the barrier, scanning faces. A father pretending to be calm, holding the car keys too tight. And then the one they've waited for walks through, and for a few minutes nobody can speak. Plenty of families who have sent someone far away know that hall. In the janamsakhis, Guru Nanak's parents get their arrivals hall too, on the edge of their own village. And the hardest part comes after the hug. Today: home to Talwandi.
screen: `THE ARRIVALS HALL.` → `A FAMILY THAT WAITED.` → `THE HARDEST PART COMES AFTER.`

segments.voice: Talwandi was the village where Nanak was born, where, tradition says, his father, Mehta Kalu, kept the village accounts, and his mother, Mata Tripta, raised him. In the tellings, after a long stretch of travel, Nanak and Mardana come back toward it. And here's a detail some tellings keep: Nanak doesn't walk straight in. He stops outside the village and sends Mardana ahead. Word reaches the house. His mother comes running out to find him. His father follows. Tradition says they wept, and held him, and then they begged. Stay. Rest. Take up a life here, among your people. We've waited long enough. And Nanak, in the tellings, answers with love, and doesn't move. His work, he tells them, is on the road. Read it the way we learned last week. What does this story know? It knows that a call can pull against the people you love most, and that the pull is real on both sides. The parents aren't villains. Their begging is a natural thing. And Nanak's answer isn't coldness. The Guru Granth Sahib uses the language of family to speak of God, calling the Divine mother and father, kin and brother. A path that prays like that has not stopped honoring parents. Nanak has been called elsewhere, and he goes with his parents' tears still on his shoulder. Notice, too, where the larger story ends up. After the journeys, Nanak settles at Kartarpur as a householder, with family around him. The road didn't swallow the home forever. But on this day at Talwandi, it had to come first.
screen: `THE VILLAGE WHERE HE WAS BORN.` · `HIS PARENTS COME RUNNING.` · `STAY. HIS WORK IS ON THE ROAD.` · `LOVE ON BOTH SIDES OF THE CALL.` · then, large: `CALLED ELSEWHERE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: call your parents or elders. Use the sit to get ready. Settle and breathe. Bring to mind a parent, a grandparent, an aunt, a teacher, an older neighbor, whoever waited on your arrivals. If they're gone, bring their face to mind and remember one thing they used to say. If they're here, decide when today you'll call. Not for news. Just to let them hear your voice. If you pray, you can say Waheguru with them in mind. The bell holds the time.
Home to Talwandi. Nanak returns to his birthplace, his parents beg him to stay, and he tells them his work is on the road.
Your line: called elsewhere. Today, make the call, and if anything is pulling you away from someone you love, say so to them gently. Day seven hundred thirty.

731.title: Kauda and the oil
731.hook: tradition says a man-eating tribesman tried to boil Nanak in oil, and the oil turned cool
731.howItsDone: Sikhs tell the sakhi of Kauda to children and in katha as a story of the Guru's calm and protection, and of a feared man who was changed rather than destroyed.

segments.voice: Yesterday, home to Talwandi, and your line, called elsewhere. Did you make the call, and did anyone's voice surprise you? Day seven hundred thirty-one.

Somewhere far from home, the fire is already lit. A great iron pan sits over it, full of oil, and the oil is starting to shimmer. A man named Kauda tends it. The tellings call him a man-eater, a wild and feared figure of the forest, and he has already seized Mardana. That's where this sakhi opens: not with Nanak preaching, but with Mardana in danger and the oil getting hot. Yesterday the Guru left his parents for the road. Today the road turns frightening. Today: Kauda and the oil.
screen: `THE FIRE IS ALREADY LIT.` → `MARDANA IS SEIZED.` → `THE ROAD TURNS FRIGHTENING.`

segments.voice: In the janamsakhis, Mardana has wandered off, and Kauda catches him. Nanak comes looking, and finds his friend about to be thrown in. Tellings differ on what comes next. In the one followed here, Kauda turns on Nanak instead. He seizes the Guru and drops him into the pan. And here's the wonder at the heart of it: tradition says the oil went cool. Nanak sits in it unharmed. Kauda stokes the fire, and still the oil won't burn him. And Kauda, the terror of the forest, stares, and then falls at the Guru's feet. The tellings say he changed his ways and began to remember the Name. Now ask what this story knows. Notice what Nanak doesn't do. He doesn't fight Kauda. He doesn't curse him or call down fire. The heat in the scene is all Kauda's: the fire, the pan, the hunger, the fear he spreads. And the Guru meets all that heat with a stillness so complete that it cools the oil itself. Read as a wonder, it shows the Guru's protection. Read as a picture, it shows what a calm person does to a burning room. Either way, the story ends with Kauda changed, not destroyed. We've seen that shape before on the road: the fiercest person in the story becomes a seeker by the end. Some readers see in Kauda's oil a picture of what the Guru's word can do to the fire inside a person: cool it, without destroying the person.
screen: `MARDANA SEIZED, THE OIL HEATING.` · `THE GURU IN THE PAN, UNHARMED.` · `NO FIGHT, NO CURSE.` · `THE FIERCE ONE BECOMES A SEEKER.` · then, large: `THE OIL WENT COOL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: cool one heated situation. Settle and breathe slowly. Bring to mind something hot in your life right now. An argument that hasn't ended. A family chat that's gone sharp. A coworker you're bracing to face. Don't replay it. Just see the heat. Then let your breath go slower, and slower, and ask what the coolest thing you could bring to it is. Not winning. Not silence. Maybe a softer first sentence. If you pray, you can say Waheguru as you breathe out. The bell holds the time.
Kauda and the oil. The sakhi of the feared man who tried to boil Guru Nanak, and the oil that went cool.
Your line: the oil went cool. Today, when something heats up, lower your voice before you raise your point. Day seven hundred thirty-one.

732.title: The land of the enchantresses
732.hook: tradition says Mardana was bewitched in a far country and Nanak's singing set him free
732.howItsDone: Sikhs gather in gurdwaras for kirtan, singing the hymns of the Guru Granth Sahib together, and tell this sakhi as a picture of the Guru's word breaking the spells of maya.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kauda and the oil, and your line, the oil went cool. Where did a lower voice cool something down? Day seven hundred thirty-two.

A song comes on in a shop, and the man at the till starts humming without noticing. Hours later, at home, the tune is still with him. A friend hums a grandmother's lullaby, and a grown woman is suddenly six years old. Songs get into people in ways arguments rarely do. The janamsakhis knew that. Mardana, the Guru's companion, was a musician, and in today's sakhi he gets into trouble in a far country, the kind of trouble no argument can get him out of. Today: the land of the enchantresses.
screen: `A SONG IN A SHOP.` → `SONGS GET IN WHERE ARGUMENTS DON'T.` → `MARDANA IN A FAR COUNTRY.`

segments.voice: In the tellings, Nanak and Mardana come to a country ruled by women, a land famous for magic. Mardana, hungry, goes ahead to find food. And he doesn't come back. A woman there has cast a spell on him. Some tellings say she turned him into a ram, tied up with a thread. Others simply say he lost himself, forgot who he was and why he'd come. Nanak goes looking. He finds his friend bound and bewildered. And what does the Guru do? He doesn't argue with the spell. He sings. Tradition says the sound of the Guru's hymn broke the enchantment, and Mardana came back to himself. Then the women of that land try their arts on Nanak. Charms, threads, spells, and in some tellings riches and beauty offered by their queen. None of it holds him. He keeps singing. And the tellings end with the enchantresses listening, and changed. So what does this story know? Some hear a plain wonder: the Guru's power over magic. Some readers also hear quieter spells in it: the pull of wanting, of distraction, of forgetting who you are. The Gurus' hymns have a name for that pull: maya. And the story's answer isn't a lecture. It's kirtan, the singing of the Guru's word, the same singing that fills a gurdwara today. Mardana's own instrument, the rabab, sits at the beginning of that song.
screen: `A COUNTRY FAMOUS FOR MAGIC.` · `MARDANA LOSES HIMSELF.` · `THE GURU SINGS, THE SPELL BREAKS.` · `KIRTAN, ANSWER TO MAYA.` · then, large: `SINGING SETS FREE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sing someone out of a mood. Start with yourself. Settle and breathe. Let a song come to mind, a hymn if you have one, a lullaby, any tune that once brought you back to yourself. Hum it under your breath, or just hear it inside. Then think of someone who seems stuck today, under some spell of gloom or worry. Ask what tune might reach them. If you pray, you can let the tune carry Waheguru. The bell holds the time.
The land of the enchantresses. The sakhi where Mardana is bewitched in a far country, and the Guru's singing sets him free.
screen: `THE LAND OF THE ENCHANTRESSES — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: singing sets free. Today, send someone a song, or hum one near them, and let the tune do what the argument can't. Day seven hundred thirty-two.

733.title: The bitter fruit made sweet
733.hook: tradition says a hungry Mardana ate bitter soapnuts at Nanak's word and found them sweet
733.howItsDone: Sikhs tell the reetha sakhi as a story of trust and gratitude, and tradition links a gurdwara in the hills, named for the reetha tree, to it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the land of the enchantresses, and your line, singing sets free. Did a tune reach someone, or reach you? Day seven hundred thirty-three.

Soapnuts. Some people still use them for laundry: small brown shells, dropped into a cloth bag, tossed in the wash, and they foam like soap. They aren't food. They're bitter enough to make a whole face fold up. Hold on to that, because in today's sakhi, a starving man is told to eat them. Yesterday Mardana was freed by a song. Today he's in the hills, hungry again, and the only food in sight grows on the wrong tree. Today: the bitter fruit made sweet.
screen: `SOAPNUTS: FOR LAUNDRY.` → `BITTER ENOUGH TO FOLD A FACE.` → `A HUNGRY MAN, THE WRONG TREE.`

segments.voice: In the tellings, Nanak and Mardana are walking through wild hill country, far from any village. Mardana is hungry, and says so, the way he does more than once in these stories. He's the very human one on the road, the one who gets tired and wants his dinner. Nanak points to a tree. It's a reetha, a soapnut tree. Eat, he says. Mardana hesitates. Soapnuts are bitter, and he knows it. But he trusts the Guru, picks one, and bites. And tradition says it was sweet. Sweet enough to fill him. Tradition links a gurdwara in those hills to this story, and it carries the tree's name. Now ask what the story knows. It knows something about hunger and about trust. Mardana doesn't get a feast. He gets the plain thing in front of him, the thing he'd have walked past. And it's the Guru's word that changes the taste. The Gurus' hymns speak of the Name as sweet. They speak of accepting what comes as the sweet will of God. So the sakhi turns that teaching into fruit. However the wonder is held, the scene makes a plain point: the same bite can taste bitter or sweet depending on what's brought to it. Met with complaint, it's soap. Received with thanks, in the Guru's name, it fed a hungry man. The sakhi doesn't ask Mardana to pretend the fruit isn't bitter. It asks him to take one bite.
screen: `HUNGRY IN THE HILLS.` · `EAT FROM THE SOAPNUT TREE.` · `TRUST, THEN A SWEET BITE.` · `THE SAME BITE, BITTER OR SWEET.` · then, large: `BITTER MADE SWEET.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: eat something plain with thanks. If you have food nearby, take one plain thing: a piece of bread, a few grains of rice, a cracker, a glass of water. If not, simply remember the last plain thing you ate. Settle and breathe. Take it slowly. Notice the taste before you judge it. Then give thanks for it, out loud or inside, as if it were the best thing on the table. If you pray, you can say Waheguru before the first bite. The bell holds the time.
The bitter fruit made sweet. Mardana, hungry in the hills, eats soapnuts at the Guru's word, and tradition says they were sweet.
screen: `THE BITTER FRUIT MADE SWEET — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: bitter made sweet. Today, when you're handed something you didn't want, a task, a meal, a change of plan, take one bite of it with thanks before you complain. Day seven hundred thirty-three.

734.title: The yogis' seat
734.hook: tradition says the Gorakhnath yogis' center later took Nanak's name, Nanakmata
734.howItsDone: Sikhs visit Gurdwara Nanakmata Sahib as a place of pilgrimage and tell the sakhi of the yogis' seat and the pipal tree that turned green.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the bitter fruit made sweet, and your line, bitter made sweet. What did you take one thankful bite of? Day seven hundred thirty-four.

A campsite sign: leave it better than you found it. A rental flat with a note on the fridge from the last guests, thanking whoever comes next. Some places even take the name of a visitor who changed them. That's today's sakhi. The road has carried Guru Nanak and Mardana through oil and enchantment and bitter fruit. Now it brings them to a seat that belonged to someone else, a center of yogis, and a place that would one day carry a new name. Today: the yogis' seat.
screen: `LEAVE IT BETTER THAN YOU FOUND IT.` → `A PLACE TAKES A VISITOR'S NAME.` → `A SEAT THAT BELONGED TO OTHERS.`

segments.voice: The yogis in this story followed Gorakhnath, the teacher their order looks back to, and their center in the foothills was known by his name, Gorakhmata. We've met Gorakhnath's yogis before this year, on the mountain and at Achal, asking Nanak hard questions. Here, tradition says, the Guru comes to their own home ground and sits down under a dry, dead pipal tree. And the tree turns green. The yogis are not pleased to find a stranger on their seat. The tellings show them trying their powers to move him, and failing, and then sitting down to talk. And the talk does what talk does in these sakhis. Some of them stay to listen. In time, tradition says, the place itself took the Guru's name: Nanakmata. A gurdwara stands there now, and Sikhs go there as pilgrims. Here's what the story knows. Notice the tree. Nanak doesn't take the yogis' seat by force, and he doesn't tear anything down. The dead tree comes back to life where he sits. The tree is greener after he sits there. The story doesn't mock the yogis; Guru Nanak treated them as serious seekers, worth arguing with because they were in earnest. His hymns ask them to carry their discipline inward, to make contentment their earrings and the Name their practice. That's a visitor who leaves a place better: not by erasing what was there, but by making something grow where he sat.
screen: `GORAKHMATA, THE YOGIS' CENTER.` · `A DEAD TREE TURNS GREEN.` · `THE PLACE TAKES A NEW NAME.` · `NOT ERASED, BROUGHT BACK TO LIFE.` · then, large: `LEAVE IT BETTER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: leave a place better. Use the sit to choose it. Settle and breathe, and look around you, or think of where you'll be in an hour. A kitchen. A desk. A bus seat. A park bench. A shared bathroom. Pick one place and one small thing: a wiped counter, a picked-up wrapper, a chair pushed in, a note of thanks. Something the next person will find without knowing who did it. If you pray, you can say Waheguru as you picture it done. The bell holds the time.
The yogis' seat. Gorakhmata, the yogis' center where tradition says a dead tree turned green under Nanak, and which came to be called Nanakmata.
Your line: leave it better. Today, do that one small thing in one shared place, and walk away without signing it. Day seven hundred thirty-four.

735.title: Cooking at the eclipse
735.hook: at Kurukshetra Nanak cooked food on an eclipse day, and tradition says he answered the objections with a hymn
735.howItsDone: Sikhs tell the Kurukshetra sakhi as an example of Guru Nanak questioning rituals by asking what they are for, and Sikh teaching places inner truth above outward observance.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the yogis' seat, and your line, leave it better. Which shared place did you leave a little better, unsigned? Day seven hundred thirty-five.

Look back over this week's road. Sri Chand, a different path. Home to Talwandi, called elsewhere. Kauda, and the oil went cool. The enchantresses, and singing sets free. The soapnuts, bitter made sweet. Gorakhmata, leave it better. Today the road ends the week in a crowd. A huge gathering of pilgrims has come to a holy place on a day when the sun is about to go dark. And in the middle of it all, a traveler lights a cooking fire. Today: cooking at the eclipse.
screen: `A WEEK ON THE ROAD.` → `A CROWD, A DARKENING SUN.` → `A TRAVELER LIGHTS A FIRE.`

segments.voice: The place was Kurukshetra, a holy site where pilgrims gathered on the day of a solar eclipse to bathe and pray. The custom there held that no food should be cooked while the eclipse lasted. In the tellings, Guru Nanak and Mardana arrive, set up camp near the crowd, and Nanak starts a fire and begins to cook. Some tellings say the food was meat, given to him by a visitor. Smoke rises. People notice. Priests and pilgrims gather, upset, and the argument begins. Why would anyone cook on this of all days? And tradition says the Guru answered not with a lecture but with a hymn. The Guru Granth Sahib holds a hymn that tradition links to this moment. In paraphrase, it says that fools quarrel over flesh, but understand nothing of wisdom or meditation. Some readers hear it turning the question away from what's on the fire and toward what's in the heart. Now ask what the story knows. Notice how Nanak questions the custom. He doesn't shout from a distance or mock people at prayer. He does one small, visible thing, lets it raise the question, and then sings. The crowd comes to him, curious and angry, and leaves with something to think about. We've seen this before on his road. He questioned rituals he thought had lost their meaning, in more than one tradition, and he did it by asking what a practice is for. Sikh teaching carries that on: what matters is the inner truth a custom points to. Today's story isn't a verdict on the pilgrims. It's a picture of how to question kindly, in the middle of a crowd.
screen: `KURUKSHETRA, AN ECLIPSE DAY.` · `A COOKING FIRE IN THE CROWD.` · `THE ANSWER IS A HYMN.` · `ASK WHAT A PRACTICE IS FOR.` · then, large: `KINDLY, QUESTION IT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: question one superstition kindly. Start with your own. Settle and breathe. Find one small habit you keep without knowing why. A lucky shirt. Knocking on wood. Not saying a hope out loud in case it breaks. Don't sneer at it. Just ask it, gently, what it's for. What is it trying to protect? Is there a truer way to protect that? If you pray, you can say Waheguru as you ask. The bell holds the time.
Cooking at the eclipse. At Kurukshetra, Nanak lit a cooking fire on an eclipse day, and tradition says he answered the objections with a hymn.
Your line: kindly, question it. Today, when someone tells you how things must be done, ask what the custom is for, with curiosity, not scorn. Day seven hundred thirty-five.

fork.setup: you're at Kurukshetra on an eclipse day. the custom says no cooking. you think the custom has lost its meaning. what do you do?
options: stay quiet and keep the custom.
stand up and denounce the crowd.
light a fire, let people come, and answer with a hymn.
fork.reveal: in the tellings, Nanak cooked, the crowd gathered, and tradition says he answered with a hymn about fools who quarrel over flesh but know nothing of wisdom or meditation.

what it means: Nanak questions a custom by doing one small thing and asking, in a hymn, what the practice is for.
